summary: Defines an extension to the Management Information Base for managing the frame relay service in TCP/IP-based networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2954 defines SNMP objects for managing a frame relay network service. A customer management system can inspect logical ports and permanent virtual circuits, review counters and status, and, where supported, change selected settings.

questions: how to manage frame relay with snmp
what is the frame relay service mib
how to manage frame relay pvcs with snmp
subtitle: An SNMP MIB for monitoring frame relay service ports, virtual circuits, counters and status changes.

tldr.problem: Customers needed a standard way to monitor the configuration, performance and faults of frame relay services supplied by a network provider.
tldr.mechanism: The Frame Relay Service MIB models logical ports, signaling, PVC endpoints and connections, accounting counters and notifications as SNMP objects.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2954 obsoletes RFC 1604 and has been updated by RFC 9141. Its read-write objects can allow switch management, while a service-only view can remain read-only.

today: RFC 2954 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2000. It obsoletes RFC 1604 and has been updated by RFC 9141.

sections.title: The Service View and FRS Agent
sections.content:
The Frame Relay Service Management Information Base (MIB) supports customer network management of a provider's service. A customer's management station can monitor logical ports and permanent virtual circuits (PVCs), read configuration and performance information, and detect faults. Some agents may also let customers create, modify, activate or deactivate PVCs.

The MIB models all the customer's delivered interfaces and PVCs as one virtual SNMP system, even when they exist on several physical devices. The agent providing this service view is called a Frame Relay Service (FRS) agent. Internal switches, line cards, routing tables and the physical layer are outside the MIB's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB gives a customer a single SNMP view of its provider's frame relay service. It describes service interfaces and circuits, not the provider's internal equipment.

sections.title: Ports, Circuits and Service Boundaries
sections.content:
A logical port represents a frame relay interface. A PVC is a virtual connection whose endpoints and bearer capabilities are set when the service is subscribed to. A PVC segment is the portion of that connection within one frame relay network.

This MIB covers one provider's service. If a PVC crosses multiple provider networks, the customer must query a different FRS agent in each network to assemble the end-to-end view. The provider should limit each subscriber's MIB view to that subscriber's own interfaces and PVCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each provider's agent describes only its own part of a circuit. A customer must query each provider separately when a PVC crosses multiple networks.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
The Frame Relay Service MIB works with the standard Interfaces MIB. A frame relay service interface uses ifType value 44, and the interface stack group shows how that logical interface relates to lower interfaces such as DS0 or DS1. Generic interface counters describe the port; this MIB provides counters for individual virtual connections.

A connection that crosses from frame relay to ATM is represented in the separate Frame Relay/ATM PVC Service Interworking MIB, not in this MIB's frame relay connection table. The FRS agent can be accessed over a PVC using SNMP over UDP over IP carried in frame relay.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB extends the standard interface view with frame relay details and circuit-level counters. A circuit that crosses into ATM is recorded in a separate interworking MIB.

sections.title: Logical Ports and Signaling
sections.content:
The logical-port table records details such as the port's UNI or NNI role, numbering plan, Q.922 address and DLCI length, and the local in-channel signaling protocol. A second table exposes signaling parameters, timers and error counters. Some administrative objects can set port type, signaling protocol and fragmentation controls.

The MIB also defines a hint for a free DLCI index to use when creating a PVC endpoint. The signaling table combines parameters for the supported protocols; an older pointer object is deprecated because the parameters are now held in one table.
sections.plainLanguage: Each logical port has a record describing its role and signaling setup. Depending on the agent's compliance level, authorized managers may change some settings.

sections.title: Creating and Monitoring PVCs
sections.content:
A PVC endpoint is identified by a logical-port index and a DLCI index. Its row records traffic parameters in both directions, such as maximum frame size, committed and excess burst sizes, and committed information rate. It also exposes frame, octet, discard and congestion counters.

To create a connection, first create the endpoint rows and their parameters. Then obtain a connection index, join the endpoint rows in the PVC connection table, and activate the connection. The table records operational status separately for each direction. Not every implementation supports creating or modifying PVCs through SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: First create and describe the two endpoints. Then connect them in the MIB and activate the circuit; the agent reports status for each direction.

sections.title: Accounting and Notifications
sections.content:
Accounting tables count segments sent and received for each PVC endpoint or logical port. A notification reports when a PVC changes state and includes its directional status and received signaling status. A logical-port link-up or link-down notification is used if the frame relay UNI changes state.

The revised notification replaces an earlier form that included redundant index values. The RFC defines separate conformance modules for a read-only customer service view and a switch-management view with administrative controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Accounting counters summarize segments by circuit or port. Notifications report circuit state changes, while a link notification reports a port failure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Read-write and read-create objects can affect network operation if they are changed without protection. The MIB does not contain sensitive information, but its community table and service controls still require appropriate access limits.

The RFC recommends SNMPv3's User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model. The customer or user is responsible for configuring access so only authorized principals can read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Unprotected write access could disrupt the service. Configure SNMP access so only authorized users can view or change the MIB objects.
